evidence_items.excerpt_or_paraphrase: Bangla is fundamentally a head-final, Subject-Object-Verb (SOV) language where verbs occupy the final position in unmarked matrix declarative clauses.
evidence_items.notes: Establishes canonical constituent hierarchy in BDSB standard.

evidence_items.excerpt_or_paraphrase: While SOV is underlying and canonical, constituent order is flexible and permits leftward and rightward movement (OSV, OVS, VSO) conditioned by pragmatic focus, topicalization, and discourse emphasis without altering core thematic role assignments.
evidence_items.notes: Generative syntactic account of scrambling in Bangla syntax.

evidence_items.locator: Chapter 4 (Nouns and Case), Section 4.3 (Objective Case), pp. 62–66
evidence_items.excerpt_or_paraphrase: Direct objects in Bangla exhibit Differential Object Marking (DOM): animate and definite direct objects obligatorily take the accusative inflection suffix -ke, whereas inanimate and indefinite direct objects remain unmarked in the zero/direct case.
evidence_items.notes: Definitive descriptive formulation of animacy-conditioned DOM.

evidence_items.excerpt_or_paraphrase: Because verbal inflection suffixes unambiguously encode grammatical person and honorific status, overt subject pronouns are frequently omitted (pro-drop) in discourse contexts where the referent is pragmatically accessible.
evidence_items.notes: Morphosyntactic basis of pro-drop in BDSB.

evidence_items.excerpt_or_paraphrase: Experiencer predicates involving physical sensation, psychological state, obligation, or modal necessity assign Dative/Genitive case to the subject argument (e.g. 'Amar khide peyeche', 'Ta-ke jete hobe'), with the verb showing neutral 3rd person non-honorific agreement.
evidence_items.notes: Syntactic analysis of non-nominative experiencer subjects.

evidence_items.excerpt_or_paraphrase: Bangla pronouns encode a mandatory tri-partite honorific distinction in the 2nd person (Apni [Honorific], Tumi [Familiar], Tui [Intimate]) and a binary honorific distinction in the 3rd person (Tini/Uni [Honorific] vs Se/E/O [Ordinary]), strictly governing verbal person suffixes.
evidence_items.notes: Establishes BDSB standard honorific pronominal paradigms.

evidence_items.excerpt_or_paraphrase: Simple present tense suffixes affix directly to verbal stems according to person: 1st person takes -i, 2nd ordinary takes -o, 2nd honorific takes -en, 2nd intimate takes -is, 3rd ordinary takes -e, and 3rd honorific takes -en.
evidence_items.notes: Finite simple present inflectional matrix.

evidence_items.excerpt_or_paraphrase: Continuous aspect is formed by adding the aspectual marker -ch- to the verb root followed by personal endings (e.g. khor-ch-i, khor-ch-en). In past continuous, the past marker -il- follows -ch- (e.g. khor-ch-il-am).
evidence_items.notes: Continuous aspect inflectional architecture in Cholit standard.

evidence_items.excerpt_or_paraphrase: Future tense is formed by adding the future infix -b- to the verb root with person-specific endings: 1st person takes -bo, 2nd ordinary takes -be, 2nd honorific takes -ben, 2nd intimate takes -bi, 3rd ordinary takes -be, and 3rd honorific takes -ben.
evidence_items.notes: Future tense paradigm in BDSB standard.

evidence_items.excerpt_or_paraphrase: The standard sentential negator 'na' occurs strictly post-verbally in finite matrix clauses ('Ami jani na'). Pre-verbal negation is restricted to non-finite subordinate clauses, conditional protases ('Jodi na jao'), or emphatic topical fronting.
evidence_items.notes: Syntactic placement rules for sentential negator 'na'.

evidence_items.excerpt_or_paraphrase: To negate an action completed in the past or present perfect, the particle 'ni' is attached to the simple present tense finite verb (e.g. 'Ami jaini' = 'I have not gone / I did not go'), completely replacing the past tense verb + 'na' combination in standard spoken and written BDSB.
evidence_items.notes: Morphosyntactic distribution of the perfective negator 'ni'.

evidence_items.excerpt_or_paraphrase: Bangla differentiates equational/identificational negation from existential/locative/possessive negation: 'noy' negates identity/classification ('Tini shikkhok non'), whereas 'nei' negates existence, location, or possession ('Bari-te keu nei', 'Amar somoy nei').
evidence_items.notes: Distinction between copular negators 'noy' and 'nei'.

evidence_items.excerpt_or_paraphrase: Compound verb constructions consist of a pole verb in the conjunctive participle (-e) combined with an inflected vector/auxiliary verb (e.g. phela, neoa, dewa, utha, bosha) that contributes telicity, self-benefit, other-benefit, spontaneity, or completion without adding a new thematic argument.
evidence_items.notes: Semantic and structural taxonomy of Bangla vector verbs.

evidence_items.excerpt_or_paraphrase: Numeral classifiers are enclitics affixed either directly to numerals (e.g. 'tin-ti boi', 'ek-jon manush') to form quantified noun phrases, or attached directly to nouns (e.g. 'boi-ta') to mark definiteness and individuation.
evidence_items.notes: Dual function of classifiers as quantification counters and definiteness markers.

evidence_items.excerpt_or_paraphrase: Postpositions in Bangla fall into three distinct governing classes: (1) Genitive-governing postpositions requiring -r/-er on their noun complement (e.g. jonno, shathe, pore, kache), (2) Locative-governing postpositions, and (3) Direct postpositions governing unmarked direct noun forms (e.g. chhara, porjonto).
evidence_items.notes: Syntactic classification of postpositional case governance.

evidence_items.excerpt_or_paraphrase: Polar (yes/no) questions are formed using the interrogative particle 'ki' placed immediately before the finite verb or in pre-predicate position with rising intonation, distinct from the in-situ content Wh-word 'ki' ('what').
evidence_items.notes: Distinction between polar interrogative particle 'ki' and Wh-pronoun 'ki'.

evidence_items.excerpt_or_paraphrase: Plurality marking is differentiated by animacy and honorificity: human nouns take animate plural suffixes -ra/-era (e.g. 'manush-era', 'chhele-ra'), whereas inanimate and non-human entities take non-personal collective enclitics -gulo/-gula/-shob (e.g. 'boi-gulo').
evidence_items.notes: Animacy constraints governing nominal plural inflection in BDSB.

evidence_items.excerpt_or_paraphrase: Habitual past tense is formed by infixing -t- to the verb root with personal endings (e.g. 'kortam', 'korte', 'korten'), expressing repeated past action, past state, or counterfactual conditional apodoses.
evidence_items.notes: Morphology and semantic dual-use of past habitual in counterfactuals.

evidence_items.excerpt_or_paraphrase: Conditional subordinate clauses in Bangla are formed with the conditional participle suffix -le attached to the verb root in the protasis (e.g. 'Tumi ele ami jabo'), or with correlative conjunctions 'jodi ... tobe/tahole'.
evidence_items.notes: Synthetic and analytic conditional clause structures in BDSB.

evidence_items.excerpt_or_paraphrase: Relative clauses in Bangla use the correlative strategy with J-initial relative pronouns/adverbs in the subordinate clause matched by T-initial demonstratives/correlatives in the main clause ('Je porishrom kore, she shofol hoy').
evidence_items.notes: Correlative J-/T- relative clause architecture in Bangla syntax.

evidence_items.excerpt_or_paraphrase: Bangla utilizes bound enclitics for information structure: '-i' conveys exclusive, restrictive, or intensifying focus ('only/very'), whereas '-o' conveys inclusive, additive, or scalar focus ('also/even').
evidence_items.notes: Focus and additive enclitics distribution in BDSB.
